transcript.speaker: Resident
transcript.text: Good afternoon, Mr. Hassan. Thank you for coming back in to see us today.

transcript.speaker: Patient
transcript.text: I'm here. Not that I expected much from this visit.

transcript.speaker: Resident
transcript.text: I want to start by talking about what happened during your admission last week. I've reviewed your charts and the triage notes.

transcript.speaker: Patient
transcript.text: I'm sure you have. Is this the part where you tell me everything was actually fine and I just imagine things?

transcript.speaker: Resident
transcript.text: No, it wasn't fine. There was a mistake in how your case was handled when you first arrived. You were triaged as low-acuity, which means the staff didn't mark your symptoms as urgent. Because of that, the imaging was delayed. By the time we got the scans, the window to give you the clot-busting medication, the thrombolysis, had already closed.

transcript.speaker: Patient
transcript.text: So you're saying you just... missed the window?

transcript.speaker: Resident
transcript.text: Yes, that's exactly what happened. We didn't get you into the scanner fast enough because the priority level was set wrong at the start. Does that make sense, or can I clarify any of that?

transcript.speaker: Patient
transcript.text: It makes perfect sense. It's the same thing every time I even step foot in this building. Just another mistake on the list.

transcript.speaker: Resident
transcript.text: I am sorry for this. It was our responsibility to get your triage right and we failed to do that.

transcript.speaker: Patient
transcript.text: Sorry. Right. I've heard sorry from three different departments in two years. It doesn't actually change the fact that my left side doesn't work the way it used to.

transcript.speaker: Resident
transcript.text: I know that an apology doesn't fix the physical impact this has had on you.

transcript.speaker: Patient
transcript.text: No, it doesn't. It really doesn't. I'm just tired of being the one who has to keep track of your errors for you.

transcript.speaker: Resident
transcript.text: It sounds like you're feeling exhausted and just completely fed up with the way you've been treated.

transcript.speaker: Patient
transcript.text: Exhausted doesn't even cover it. I feel like a glitch in your system.

transcript.speaker: Resident
transcript.text: I hear you. I can't undo the delay, but I want to make sure we are moving forward correctly now.

transcript.speaker: Patient
transcript.text: If you can.

transcript.speaker: Resident
transcript.text: Here is the plan for the next two weeks. First, I'm referring you to the neuro-rehabilitation team. I'm putting that request in right now, and you should receive a phone call from them by Thursday to schedule your first assessment. Your role is to keep a log of any new weakness you feel in your arm so you can show the therapist. Then, I want to see you back here in exactly fourteen days to review those results. Does that timeline work for you?

transcript.speaker: Patient
transcript.text: I guess. As long as I don't have to spend six hours in the waiting room again.

transcript.speaker: Resident
transcript.text: I'll make a note on your file to ensure we prioritize your check-in for this follow-up.

transcript.speaker: Patient
transcript.text: We'll see.

transcript.speaker: Resident
transcript.text: I understand if you're skeptical. I'm going to provide you with a written summary of what we've discussed today and the contact details for the rehab coordinator.

transcript.speaker: Patient
transcript.text: Fine. Just give me the paper.

H.justification: Resident never interrupts, remains regulated despite patient's skepticism, and allows the patient to express frustration without rushing.

E.justification: Error named in the second turn, uses lay language ('clot-busting medication'), checks comprehension ('Does that make sense?'), and avoids false reassurance.

A.justification: Direct apology used ('I am sorry'), explicitly takes responsibility ('we failed to do that'), and maintains accountability despite patient pushback.

R.justification: Resident names a specific emotion ('exhausted and just completely fed up') and engages the patient's emotional bids, but only does so once.

T.justification: Provides specific next steps (neuro-rehab) with a timeline (by Thursday/14 days) and a patient role (keep a log), but does not address systemic prevention of the error.
